reason: The text presents the opposite dynamic. The passage (Nehemiah 5) depicts regular people rightfully complaining about economic oppression and exploitation by their leaders—the nobles and magistrates who were exacting usury, seizing fields, and enslaving their children. Nehemiah, the protagonist leader, validates their grievance ('my heart was very angry when I heard their outcry') and rebukes the corrupt rulers, commanding them to restore the people's property and cancel their debts. The narrative explicitly positions the people as victims of injustice and the previous governors as oppressors. Nehemiah then contrasts himself favorably with prior governors, showing he deliberately refused to burden the people 'out of fear of God.' The story concludes with the people praising God and the assembly affirming Nehemiah's righteous redistribution. The entire arc vindicates the common people and condemns corrupt leadership.
